11300:
When something is notable, it means it is worth noticing and worth remembering — it stands out from the ordinary in a way that deserves your attention. Think of it this way: out of a hundred things happening around you, most fade into the background. A notable thing refuses to fade. It rises above the rest and demands to be acknowledged.

The word essentially says: "Pay attention to this. This one matters."
Two Main Ways It Is Used

Notable is used in two closely related situations:

1. To describe a thing, event, quality, or fact that is impressive or significant

Here, notable means the thing has a quality that makes it stand out clearly from what is typical or expected.

"She made a notable improvement in her grades this semester."

(Her improvement wasn't small or ordinary — it was significant enough that people would notice and remember it.)

"There was a notable difference in temperature between the two rooms."

(The difference wasn't subtle — it was clear and striking enough to catch attention.)

"The speech contained several notable ideas."

(The ideas weren't just average thoughts — they were meaningful, interesting, and worth keeping in mind.)

2. To describe a person who is well-known, respected, or distinguished

Here, notable describes someone who has earned a level of recognition or standing that puts them above the average person in their field or community.

"Several notable scientists attended the conference."

(These weren't unknown or ordinary scientists — they were recognized, respected figures.)

"The town has produced many notable artists over the years."

(Artists who became known and celebrated, not those who remained obscure.)

Something becomes notable when it crosses an invisible line — when it goes from being ordinary or forgettable to being significant, impressive, or clearly different in some way. That crossing can happen in several ways:

  • Size or degree: A temperature drop of 1°C is ordinary. A drop of 20°C overnight is notable.
  • Achievement or quality: Finishing a race is ordinary. Finishing first after training for only a month is notable.
  • Rarity: A sunny day in summer is ordinary. A sunny day in the middle of a long winter is notable.
  • Recognition: A local worker is ordinary. A Nobel Prize winner is a notable figure.

The key is that something has risen clearly enough above the common level that people take notice.

Notable sits in the middle range of strength. It is a genuine compliment or acknowledgment, but it is not the strongest word in this family. Think of it on a scale:

Ordinary → Worth mentioning → Notable → Remarkable → Extraordinary

So when you call something notable, you are saying it genuinely stands out and deserves recognition — but you are not claiming it is the most incredible thing ever. It is a measured, thoughtful word. This is actually one of its strengths: it sounds credible and precise, not exaggerated.

One of the most frequent ways you will encounter this word is in the phrase "notable exception" or "with a few notable exceptions."

"The students all performed well, with a few notable exceptions."

This means: most students performed well, but a small number stood out — in this case, by not following the pattern. Their performance was different enough to deserve special mention.

This usage shows that notable doesn't always mean good — it simply means standing out in a way that demands attention, whether that standing out is positive, negative, or neutral.
The Tone and Register of the Word

Notable has a slightly formal, composed tone. You are more likely to see it in:

  • News articles and journalism
  • Academic writing
  • Professional reports
  • Formal speeches

In casual everyday conversation, people more often say things like "impressive," "worth mentioning," or "a big deal" instead of "notable." But "notable" is not so formal that it sounds strange in everyday writing — it is a perfectly natural word in most contexts.
Close Relatives (Synonyms) and How They Differ

Understanding how notable compares to similar words will sharpen your understanding of it:

  • Noteworthy — Almost identical in meaning. Slightly more formal. Interchangeable with notable in most cases.
  • Remarkable — A step stronger. Suggests something is so unusual or impressive that it prompts comment or reaction.
  • Significant — Focuses more on importance and consequences than on being noticed. A notable fact catches your eye; a significant fact changes how you think or act.
  • Prominent — More about visibility or position. A prominent person stands in the public eye. A notable person has earned recognition through achievement or quality.
  • Distinguished — Used almost exclusively for people. It suggests a long history of earned respect and a high level of prestige.
  • Outstanding — Stronger than notable. Suggests excellence that clearly surpasses others.
  • Eminent — Used for people. Suggests fame and high standing within a profession or field, typically built over a long career.

Among all of these, notable is the most versatile and the most moderate — precise without being extreme, respectful without being lavish.

What it meansWorth noticing; standing clearly above the ordinary; deserving to be remembered or acknowledged
Used forThings (achievements, differences, features, changes) and people (well-known, respected figures)
StrengthMedium — genuine and credible, but not superlative
ToneSlightly formal, but widely usable
Key phrase"Notable exception" — something that stands out by not following the common pattern

In one sentence: if something is notable, it has risen far enough above the ordinary that the world pauses to take notice — and rightly so.
11301:
To notarize a document means to have it officially certified by a specially licensed official called a notary public, so that the world — including courts, banks, and government offices — can trust that the document is genuine.

When you notarize something, you are essentially adding a layer of official proof to it. That proof says: "A real, qualified, government-authorized person witnessed this. The signatures on it are genuine. The people who signed it are who they say they are. This document was not faked, forged, or signed under pressure."

Before you can fully understand "notarize," you need to know what a notary public is, because the entire act of notarizing revolves around this person.

A notary public (often just called a "notary") is a person officially authorized by the government — usually at the state or regional level — to serve as a trusted, neutral, legal witness. They are not a judge. They are not necessarily a lawyer. Think of them as an official human stamp of trust. Banks, post offices, law offices, and courts often have them. Their job is to verify that important documents are signed properly and honestly.
What Actually Happens When You Notarize a Document?

Here is the process, step by step, so you can see exactly what "notarizing" involves in the real world:

Step 1 — You bring your document to a notary. You take the unsigned (or sometimes already signed) document to a notary public in person. Increasingly, remote online notarization (RON) is also allowed in many places, where this happens via a secure video call.

Step 2 — You prove who you are. The notary asks you to show a valid, government-issued photo ID — like a passport or a driver's license. This is a critical step. The notary needs to confirm you are actually the person named in the document, not someone pretending to be you.

Step 3 — The notary confirms you are acting freely. The notary asks you a few questions to make sure you understand what you are signing and that nobody is forcing or pressuring you to sign it. You must be of sound mind and acting voluntarily.

Step 4 — You sign the document in the notary's presence. (In some cases, if you already signed it, you may acknowledge to the notary that the signature is yours.)

Step 5 — The notary signs, stamps, and seals. The notary then signs the document themselves and applies their official notary seal (sometimes called a notary stamp). This seal typically shows the notary's name, their official ID or commission number, their jurisdiction, and their commission expiration date. This seal is the physical mark that transforms an ordinary document into a notarized one.

Step 6 — The notary records it in their journal. Most notaries are required by law to keep an official logbook (called a notary journal or notary register) where they record every notarization they perform. This creates a paper trail and protects against fraud.

Once all of this is done, the document is said to have been notarized.
Why Does Notarizing Matter? What Does It Achieve?

Notarizing a document serves several powerful purposes:

It prevents fraud. Because the notary checks your ID and watches you sign, it becomes very hard for someone to forge signatures, impersonate another person, or submit a fake document.

It makes documents legally trustworthy. Many important documents — especially those involving large amounts of money, property, or legal rights — are required by law to be notarized before they are accepted. Without notarization, certain documents are simply not valid.

It protects all parties involved. If a dispute arises later, a notarized document carries much more legal weight than one that was not notarized. It can serve as strong evidence in court.

It acts as a deterrent. Knowing that a neutral official witnessed the signing discourages people from signing under duress or making dishonest claims later.

Not every notarization is exactly the same. Depending on the document, a notary may perform different acts:

Acknowledgment: The most common type. You appear before the notary and acknowledge (confirm) that you signed the document voluntarily and that you understand it. You do not have to sign it again in front of the notary if you already signed it — you just confirm the signature is yours.

Jurat (sworn oath/affirmation): Here, you must sign the document in front of the notary and also swear or affirm — under oath — that the contents of the document are true to the best of your knowledge. This is common for affidavits (written sworn statements). Lying in a jurat can be considered perjury.

Copy certification: The notary certifies that a photocopy of an original document is a true, accurate, unaltered copy of the original. For example, certifying a copy of a diploma or a passport.

Signature witnessing: The notary simply witnesses you signing a document without necessarily verifying the truth of its contents. The focus is purely on the authenticity of the signature.
What Documents Commonly Need to Be Notarized?

Notarization is typically required or strongly recommended for high-stakes documents. Common examples include:

  • Real estate deeds (buying or selling property)
  • Wills and trusts (legal documents about who inherits your belongings)
  • Powers of attorney (giving someone legal authority to act on your behalf)
  • Affidavits (sworn written statements of fact)
  • Loan documents and mortgages
  • Adoption papers
  • Business contracts of significant value
  • Court documents
  • International documents that need to be used in a foreign country (these often require an extra step called apostille, which further certifies the notary's credentials for international use)
Related Word Forms You Will Encounter

Since you want to be fully equipped with this word, here are the closely related forms:

  • Notarized (adjective/past tense verb) — describing a document that has already gone through the notarization process. "This is a notarized copy of my birth certificate."
  • Notarization (noun) — the act or process of notarizing. "The bank required notarization of the loan agreement."
  • Notary / Notary public (noun) — the official who performs the notarization.
How It Is Used in Sentences

• "You need to notarize the deed before the property transfer can go through."
  • "I went to the bank to notarize my signature on the power of attorney."
  • "The court will not accept any document that has not been notarized."
  • "She asked a local notary to notarize copies of her diploma for her job application abroad."
  • "The contract was signed, notarized, and filed with the county recorder's office."
A Simple Way to Remember It

If you want one clean mental image to anchor this word:

Notarize = making a document "officially witnessed and certified" by a government-authorized person, so it becomes legally trustworthy.

It is the act of going from "just a piece of paper with signatures" to "an officially verified, legally credible document."
11302: A notary — most commonly referred to as a notary public — is a person officially appointed or licensed by a government to act as an impartial, trusted witness for important legal documents and transactions. Their core job is to verify that a signature on a document is genuine, that the person signing is who they claim to be, and that they signed willingly and with full awareness of what they were signing.

The fundamental reason notaries exist is fraud prevention.

Imagine you sign a property deed or a will today, but years later someone claims you never signed it — or that your signature was forged. A notary prevents this by standing there as an official, government-recognized witness at the exact moment of signing and creating a permanent official record of what happened.

When a notary verifies a document, that document is described as notarized. A notarized document carries far stronger legal weight than an ordinary unwitnessed one, because a trusted, government-authorized third party has officially confirmed its authenticity.

A notary performs several specific official acts:

Witnessing a signature — This is the most common task. You appear before the notary, prove your identity (usually with a government-issued photo ID like a passport or driver's license), and sign your document in front of them. The notary then signs the document themselves and stamps it with their official seal. The whole process is called notarization.

Administering oaths and affirmations — A notary can legally swear you in before you make a sworn written statement (called an affidavit). Once you make a statement under oath before a notary, you are legally responsible for its truth. Lying in such a statement is a crime — the same as lying in court.

Certifying copies — A notary can officially confirm that a photocopy of an original document is a true and accurate copy of the original. This is useful when you must submit a copy of something important — like a birth certificate or a degree — to an institution, without handing over the irreplaceable original.

Acknowledging signatures — Sometimes you sign a document beforehand and then appear before the notary simply to confirm that the signature is yours and that you signed it freely, without pressure or force. This official confirmation is called an acknowledgment.

Every notary has an official seal or stamp — a physical or digital mark applied to every document they notarize. This seal typically contains the notary's full name, their official title ("Notary Public"), the jurisdiction they are authorized in (such as a state or country), and often an expiration date for their authorization.

The seal is what makes a document officially notarized. Without it, the notarial act is incomplete and not legally valid.

Notaries also maintain a record book — called a journal or register — where they log every notarization they perform: the date, the document type, the signer's name, and the ID they presented. This creates a permanent, traceable record.

A notary's official government authorization to perform notarizations is called their commission. In the United States, this is issued by a state government; in other countries, by the national or regional authority. Commissions typically have an expiration date — four years in many US states, for example — after which the notary must renew their authorization. A notary acting after their commission has expired is no longer legally authorized to notarize anything.

You typically need a notary when signing documents with serious legal or financial consequences, such as:

  • Real estate transactions — buying or selling property, mortgage agreements
  • Wills and trusts — documents directing how your assets are handled after death
  • Power of attorney — documents authorizing someone else to make legal or financial decisions on your behalf
  • Affidavits — sworn written statements used in legal proceedings
  • Business contracts — certain high-stakes agreements between parties
  • Immigration and visa documents — many countries require notarization for applications
  • Loan agreements — particularly for large amounts

This is an important distinction that many people miss.

In common law countries — such as the United States, the United Kingdom, India, Canada, and Australia — a notary is not a lawyer. They cannot give you legal advice, explain what a document's clauses mean, tell you whether you should sign something, or represent you in any legal matter. Their role is strictly and only about verifying identity, witnessing, and authenticating. If you need to understand a document's legal implications, you need a lawyer. A notary simply confirms that you signed — not what you were signing or whether you should have.

In civil law countries — much of continental Europe, Latin America, parts of Africa and Asia — a notary is a far more powerful and highly trained legal professional, often with qualifications similar to a lawyer. In these systems, a notary can draft legal documents, advise clients on legal matters, manage property transfers, and handle estate settlements. The role carries substantially more responsibility and expertise.

In recent years, many jurisdictions now permit remote online notarization (RON), where the entire notarization process happens over a secure video call rather than in person. You show your ID on camera, sign electronically, and the notary applies a digital seal. The legal outcome is the same as in-person notarization. This method has grown significantly in acceptance and is now legally recognized in a growing number of countries and US states.

If you need to use a notarized document in a foreign country, you may need an additional layer of certification called an apostille. An apostille is a certificate issued by a higher-level government authority (not the notary themselves) that verifies and authenticates the notary's own credentials — making the document legally recognized in other countries that are part of the Hague Apostille Convention. Think of it as an official "stamp of approval on the notary's stamp of approval," specifically for international use.

A notary is an officially government-appointed witness whose job is to verify your identity, watch you sign important documents, administer oaths, and certify copies — all to prevent fraud and give legal documents official credibility and enforceability. The outcome of their work is a notarized document: one bearing an official seal, backed by a certified record, and carrying far stronger legal standing than an ordinary unwitnessed document. Their precise role varies by country — limited and strictly procedural in common law countries, broader and more legal in civil law countries — but their essential function everywhere is the same: to be a trustworthy, impartial, government-authorized witness that the law can rely on.
11303:
A notary public is an officially licensed, government-appointed person whose job is to act as a neutral, trusted witness when important documents are signed — and to verify that the signing was real, voluntary, and done by the right person.

Think of them as a living stamp of authenticity. When a notary puts their official seal on a document, it tells the world: "I personally confirmed who signed this, checked their identity, made sure they weren't being forced, and watched them sign it."
Why Do They Exist?

The world depends on documents — property deeds, wills, contracts, powers of attorney, affidavits. Forging a signature on any of these can cause serious harm: someone could steal your home, drain your accounts, or make life-or-death medical decisions on your behalf without your knowledge or consent.

A notary is a fraud-prevention mechanism built into the legal system. Because they are officially appointed, personally accountable under the law, and have no personal stake in the transaction, their presence and seal give a document a higher level of legal trustworthiness. Courts and institutions around the world recognize and rely on that seal.
What a Notary Public Actually Does

A notary performs specific official acts called notarial acts. The major ones are:

Acknowledgment: The signer appears before the notary, presents ID, and confirms that they signed the document freely and willingly. The notary doesn't have to watch the actual signing — the person may have already signed — but they must confirm in person that the signature is genuine and voluntary.

Jurat: Here, the notary watches the person physically sign the document and simultaneously administers an oath or affirmation — a solemn, legally binding promise that the contents of the document are true. This is used for affidavits (sworn written statements). The key difference from an acknowledgment is that the signing and the oath happen live, right in front of the notary.

Administering Oaths and Affirmations: A notary can formally place someone under oath for legal proceedings or sworn statements, even without a document being signed. An oath invokes a higher power ("I swear"); an affirmation is a secular substitute with equal legal weight ("I affirm").

Copy Certification: The notary compares an original document to a photocopy, verifies they are identical, and certifies the copy as a true and accurate reproduction. This is often needed when you can't submit your original (for example, submitting a certified copy of a birth certificate to a foreign embassy).
How a Notary Verifies Your Identity

Before performing any notarial act, the notary must confirm that the person in front of them is who they claim to be. They typically do this by checking government-issued photo ID such as a passport, driver's license, or national identity card. In some cases, identity can be confirmed through a credible identifying witness — someone who personally knows the signer and vouches for their identity under oath.

This step is critical. The entire value of notarization rests on the notary being certain of who is signing.
The Notary's Official Tools

The Seal (or Stamp): Every notary carries an official seal — a physical stamp or embosser that imprints their name, commission number, jurisdiction, and expiration date onto the document. This seal is the mark that signals the document has been officially notarized. Without it, the notarization is generally not valid.

The Notarial Journal (or Register): Most notaries are legally required to maintain a logbook of every notarial act they perform. Each entry records the date, the type of act, the document involved, the signer's name, and the ID that was used. This journal creates a paper trail that can be referred to in court or fraud investigations long after the fact.
What a Notary Public Is NOT

This distinction is crucial and frequently misunderstood.

A notary public is not a lawyer (unless they separately hold a law degree, which is a different qualification entirely). In most countries — particularly the United States, Canada, and Australia — a notary is generally not permitted to give legal advice, explain what a document means in legal terms, tell you whether you should sign something, or help you draft legal documents.

Their role is strictly limited to identity verification, witnessing signatures, administering oaths, and document authentication. If you need someone to advise you on the legal consequences of what you're signing, that's a job for a licensed attorney — not a notary.
Who Can Become a Notary Public?

Requirements vary by country and region, but the general requirements are: being an adult, being a citizen or legal resident of the jurisdiction, having a clean criminal record, and submitting a formal application to the appropriate government authority (usually a state or regional office).

In many U.S. states, becoming a notary is a relatively straightforward process — completing an application, passing a background check, sometimes taking a short training course or exam, and paying a fee. Once approved, the person is "commissioned" (officially authorized) for a fixed term, often four years, after which they must renew their commission.
Civil Law Countries vs. Common Law Countries

The role of a notary public is not the same everywhere, and understanding this difference is important.

In common law countries (such as the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia), notaries are generally ordinary citizens with a relatively limited, administrative role. Their job is mainly to witness signatures and authenticate documents. There are many of them, and their services are affordable and widely accessible.

In civil law countries (such as France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Mexico, Brazil, and most of continental Europe and Latin America), a notary is a highly trained legal professional — comparable in status and expertise to a lawyer. These notaries are deeply involved in drafting, verifying, and finalizing major legal transactions such as buying property, forming a company, and handling estates and inheritances. They carry significantly more legal power, are far fewer in number, charge considerably higher fees, and are considered essential players in the legal process — not just witnesses.
When Would You Actually Need a Notary Public?

You would typically need a notary when dealing with: buying or selling real estate, creating a will or a power of attorney, signing a legal affidavit or sworn statement, getting documents certified for use in a foreign country, completing international adoption paperwork, certain immigration documents, some business agreements, and court-related sworn declarations.
Remote Online Notarization

In recent years, many jurisdictions have introduced Remote Online Notarization (RON), where the entire notarization process happens over a secure video call. The notary verifies your identity using digital tools, watches you sign electronically, and applies a tamper-evident digital seal to the document. It carries the same legal validity as an in-person notarization in jurisdictions where it is accepted.
The Bottom Line

A notary public is an officially government-appointed, impartial witness whose core purpose is to prevent fraud and forgery on important legal documents. They confirm your identity, make sure you are signing of your own free will, witness or acknowledge the signing, and then authenticate the document with their official seal — creating a reliable, legally recognized record that the transaction was real and legitimate. They are not lawyers and do not advise you on the law; they simply certify the facts of what happened in their presence. Their role is a foundational safeguard in legal systems around the world, ensuring that the documents that govern our most important life decisions can be trusted.
11304:
Notation means a system of symbols, signs, or marks used to represent something — ideas, quantities, sounds, movements — in a clear, compact, and agreed-upon written form.

Think of it this way: the world is full of things that are hard to express in ordinary words — a musical melody, a complex equation, a chess move, a scientific measurement. Notation solves that problem. It gives people in a field a shared "visual language" — a set of symbols where everyone agrees on what each symbol means — so that complex things can be written down, read, and understood precisely.

The most important thing to understand about notation is that it is not just any writing or scribbling. A notation is a structured system — it has rules, and every symbol in it carries a specific, agreed-upon meaning within its community or discipline.

For example, the symbols +, −, ×, =, √, and ∑ together form a part of mathematical notation. When a mathematician writes √25 = 5, every trained reader in the world understands it the same way — there's no ambiguity, no room for misinterpretation. That precision and universality is exactly what notation is designed to deliver.

Notation shows up everywhere, and each field has developed its own:

In Mathematics, notation includes symbols for operations, relationships, and quantities. "Scientific notation" specifically refers to writing very large or very small numbers in a compact form — for instance, 3,000,000 is written as 3 × 10⁶. This is far easier to work with when numbers get astronomically large or tiny.

In Music, notation refers to the written system of representing sound — the staff (the five horizontal lines), clef signs, note shapes (whole note, half note, quarter note), time signatures, and dynamic marks. A musician who can read musical notation can pick up a sheet of paper and know exactly what sounds to produce, how long to hold them, and how loudly or softly to play — all from those symbols.

In Chess, players use "algebraic notation" to record moves. A move like Nf3 means the knight (N) moved to the square f3. This allows an entire game to be written down in a small amount of space and replayed perfectly by anyone who knows the system.

In Chemistry, chemical notation uses symbols and formulas. H₂O tells a chemist — instantly and without a word of explanation — that a molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

In Computer Science, "Big O notation" (like O(n²)) is used to describe how efficiently an algorithm runs. It's not math in the everyday sense; it's a specialized symbolic language for talking about computational performance.

In Dance, there even exists a notation system called Labanotation, which uses symbols to record the movements of the human body — direction, level, body part, timing — so that choreography can be preserved on paper.

The pattern is the same in every case: a domain has complex information to express, and notation gives it a precise, efficient written language to do so.

The word "notation" carries two slightly different but related meanings depending on context:

1. A system of symbols (the main and most important meaning)

This is when "notation" refers to an entire established system. You'll see it used with a descriptive word before it: musical notation, mathematical notation, chemical notation, phonetic notation. Here, the word refers to the whole framework — the complete set of symbols and rules used in a field.

"She has been studying musical notation for months."
Here, it means the entire system of reading and writing music.

"Scientists use chemical notation to write formulas."
Here, it means the entire system of representing chemical compounds symbolically.

2. A written note or mark (a secondary, everyday meaning)

In more general, everyday use, "a notation" can simply mean a brief written note, comment, or mark that someone has added somewhere — usually to record something for later reference or to annotate something.

"The doctor made a notation in the patient's file."
"She made a notation in the margin of her textbook."

Here, it just means a short written remark or annotation. This usage is less technical. It's closest to how you might use the word "note" — but "notation" often implies it's a brief, perhaps symbolic or shorthand mark rather than a full sentence.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Intended

• If "notation" comes with a descriptor like musical, mathematical, scientific, chemical, or algebraic, it almost certainly means a system of symbols.
  • If it says "a notation" (with the article "a") and is about someone writing something down in a specific place, it usually means a written note or mark.

Notation is one of the quiet engines behind human progress. Before musical notation existed, music could only be passed down by memory and listening — oral tradition. Once it was codified into written symbols, compositions could be preserved across centuries and performed by musicians who never met the composer. Mathematical notation made it possible for complex ideas to be shared, built upon, and verified across the world. Without notation, science, music, and mathematics as we know them would be impossible.

In short: notation is humanity's way of turning complex, specialized knowledge into a written form that is compact, precise, and universally understood within a community — a visual shorthand that carries enormous meaning.
11305:
A notch is a small cut, groove, or indentation made into the surface or edge of something. Think of it as a deliberate bite taken out of an object — usually shaped like a V or a U, going into the material rather than sticking out of it.

If you've ever seen a piece of wood with a little triangular groove carved into its edge, that's a notch. If you've seen a belt with a row of small holes punched along its length, those individual holes and slots are often called notches too.

The key idea is: something is cut away or pressed in, leaving a small hollow mark.

In its most concrete sense, a notch is a physical marking cut into an object. Here's where you'll encounter it:

On everyday objects:

  • A belt has notches — those little slots you fasten the buckle into. When you tighten or loosen the belt, you move it to a different notch.
  • Old tallying sticks had notches carved into them to count things, like how many sheep passed by or how much grain was traded.
  • Ratchets and gears often have notches along their edges that allow a piece to click into place and hold.
  • The lapels of a suit jacket have what's called a notch lapel — the small triangular cut where the collar meets the lapel.

On screens and technology:

  • The small cutout at the top of certain smartphone screens — where the front camera sits — is called a notch. It's literally a section cut away from the display.

In tools and craftsmanship:

  • A notch in carpentry or woodworking is a cut made in a piece of wood so that another piece can fit into it snugly, like puzzle pieces locking together.
  • Arrows have a notch (sometimes spelled "nock") at the tail end — the small groove that grips the bowstring.

The unifying thread: In all these physical uses, a notch is always cut into something, it's small but deliberate, and it usually serves a functional purpose — to hold, mark, or fit something.

In geography, a notch refers to a narrow gap, pass, or opening between mountains or hills — essentially a natural "cut" through high terrain.

Franconia Notch is a famous mountain pass in New Hampshire, USA.

You can think of it as nature carving a notch into a mountain range, creating a narrow corridor through which people can travel. It's the same idea as the physical cut, just on a massive, natural scale.
The Figurative Meaning: A Step or Degree on a Scale

This is one of the most common ways you'll encounter "notch" in everyday English, especially in conversation.

Here, a notch means one step, level, or degree on some imaginary scale — a scale of quality, intensity, loudness, difficulty, or any other measurable quality.

Imagine a volume dial with markings on it. Each marking is a notch. Moving from one marking to the next is moving "a notch."

Examples:

  • "Could you turn the music up a notch?" — Make it a little louder.
  • "The spice level in this dish is a notch above what I can handle." — It's one step more intense than I can manage.
  • "After his promotion, he moved up a notch in the company hierarchy." — He rose one level.
  • "She was a notch better than the other candidates." — Slightly, but meaningfully, superior.

The scale isn't real or numbered — it's just a way of saying "a small but distinct step in one direction."

1. Top-notch
This means of the highest quality, the very best. If something is top-notch, it sits at the highest notch on the imaginary scale of quality.

"She's a top-notch surgeon."
"The hotel provided top-notch service."

You'll see this written both with and without a hyphen: top notch and top-notch. When used before a noun, the hyphen is standard.

2. A notch above / below
This means slightly better or slightly worse than something else — by exactly one degree.

"His cooking is a notch above restaurant quality." — It's slightly better than what most restaurants serve.
"The second film was a notch below the original." — It wasn't quite as good.

3. Another notch in one's belt (or a notch on one's belt)
This idiom means an achievement, a victory, or a conquest added to one's record. It comes from the old image of a hunter or soldier carving a notch into their belt or weapon for each kill or success.

"Winning this award was another notch in her belt." — It was one more achievement to add to her list.
"He treated his business wins like notches on his belt." — He collected them proudly as proof of his success.

Sometimes this phrase carries a slightly boastful or even negative connotation — the sense that the person is keeping score of people or wins like trophies.
Summary of All Meanings at a Glance

To wrap it up cleanly:

  • Physical notch: A small V- or U-shaped cut or groove made into an object's surface or edge, usually for a functional purpose (to count, to grip, to fit, to mark).
  • Geographic notch: A narrow natural gap or pass through mountains.
  • Figurative notch: One step or degree on an imaginary scale of quality, intensity, or level — used to describe small but real differences.
  • Top-notch: The absolute best, the highest quality.
  • A notch above/below: Slightly better or worse.
  • A notch in one's belt: An achievement or conquest added to one's record.

The word always carries the same underlying feeling: something precise, small, and purposeful — whether it's a physical mark, a geographic gap, or an abstract step up or down.
11306: Before diving into all its meanings, it helps to know what ties them together. A note is always something brief, distinct, and pointed — whether it's a piece of writing, a sound, a quality you sense, or a mark of importance. Every meaning of this word carries the idea of something small but significant, something that stands out or is worth paying attention to.
Meaning 1: A Short Piece of Writing

This is the meaning most people think of first. A note is a brief written message or record — something short and informal, not a full letter or a long document.

  • You write a note on a piece of paper and stick it to the fridge: "Gone to the market. Back by 7."
  • A student passes a note to a friend in class.
  • You jot down a quick note on your phone so you don't forget something.

The key quality here is brevity. A note is not meant to be long. It captures the essential point quickly. If you sit down and write three full pages to someone, that's a letter. If you scribble a few lines, that's a note.

Within this meaning, there are a few flavours worth knowing:

A personal note is a short, informal message written to someone you know — a thank-you note, a note of apology, a note left on someone's desk.

A note to yourself (also called a reminder note) is something you write so you remember something — a shopping list item, an idea, a phone number.

Notes (in the plural) refers to information you write down while listening to someone or reading something, so you can refer to it later. Students take notes during class. Journalists take notes during interviews. "I made notes during the lecture." These notes are a way of capturing something so it isn't lost.
Meaning 2: A Short Explanatory Comment Added to a Text

When you read a book, an article, or an official document, you sometimes see small additional explanations added alongside the main text. These are called notes.

  • A footnote is a note placed at the bottom of a page to explain a word, add extra information, or cite a source.
  • An endnote is the same kind of thing, but placed at the end of a book or chapter.
  • An editor's note is a comment added by someone who prepared the text for publishing, giving the reader useful context.

"See note 3 for a full explanation of this term."

These notes are not part of the main flow of the writing — they exist alongside it to help the reader understand something better. They are brief by nature.
Meaning 3: A Formal or Official Written Communication

In more formal or official contexts — especially in diplomacy, business, or law — a note is a written document sent from one party to another to communicate something officially.

  • Governments send each other diplomatic notes — formal written communications between countries on matters of policy.
  • "The embassy sent a strongly worded note to the foreign ministry."
  • In older legal and business language, a promissory note (often just called a note) is a written promise to pay a specific amount of money to someone by a specific date. It is a legally binding document.

Here the word has a more serious, official weight, but the core idea is the same — a written communication that conveys something concisely and on the record.
Meaning 4: A Banknote (Paper Money)

In British English especially, and widely across the world, a note is a piece of paper money — what Americans call a bill.

  • "Can you give me change? I only have a fifty-pound note."
  • "She took out a crisp hundred-rupee note from her wallet."
  • "He counted out five notes and handed them over."

A note in this sense is a physical piece of currency. It is sometimes called a banknote to be precise. Coins are not notes — notes are specifically paper currency.
Meaning 5: A Single Musical Sound

In music, a note is one individual sound of a specific pitch — the basic unit of music.

  • When a pianist presses a single key, that produces one note.
  • "She played the wrong note."
  • "The song begins with a long, held note."

A musical note has two things that define it: its pitch (how high or low the sound is — like the difference between a squeak and a rumble) and its duration (how long it lasts).

Notes also exist as written symbols on a sheet of music — the little oval shapes sitting on lines and spaces that tell a musician what sound to produce and for how long. So a "note" can refer either to the sound itself or the written symbol representing that sound.

The notes in the Western musical system have names: C, D, E, F, G, A, B — and these repeat at higher and lower pitches.

"She hit every note perfectly in the performance." Here, "hit a note" means to produce the correct pitch at the right moment.
Meaning 6: A Particular Quality, Tone, or Feeling

This is a more figurative meaning, but it is extremely common in everyday English. A note can refer to a particular quality, feeling, or mood that you sense in something — in a person's voice, in the atmosphere of a situation, in the way something is written, or even in a smell or flavour.

  • "There was a note of sadness in her voice." — Her voice had a quality that told you she was a little sad.
  • "He ended his speech on a hopeful note." — The feeling or tone at the end of his speech was hopeful.
  • "I detected a note of sarcasm in his reply." — I sensed sarcasm in how he said it.
  • "The perfume has a note of jasmine." — One of the distinct smells you can detect in it is jasmine.
  • "The evening ended on a sour note." — Things became unpleasant by the end.

This usage comes from music, where a single note creates a particular mood or feeling. When applied to life and language, a "note" captures that subtle, distinct quality that colours a situation.

Phrases like "on a high note" (ending something in a positive or successful way), "on a low note" (ending something badly or disappointingly), and "on a serious note" (shifting the tone to something more grave) all use this musical-emotional idea of a note.
Meaning 7: Importance, Distinction, or Worth Noticing

A note can also refer to significance — the quality of being important or worth attention. This meaning is less about something you write or hear, and more about status or worthiness.

  • "Nothing of note happened today." — Nothing significant or worth mentioning happened.
  • "She is a writer of note." — She is a notable, distinguished, well-regarded writer.
  • "He is a scholar of some note." — He has a certain reputation and importance in his field.
  • "The meeting produced nothing of note." — The meeting produced no results worth paying attention to.

Here, a person or thing "of note" is one that stands out — one that deserves to be noticed and remembered.
Important Phrases and Expressions Built Around "Note"

Since you want to know everything about this word, here are the key fixed expressions that use "note" as a noun:

Take note (or take note of something): To pay careful attention to something; to consciously register it.
"Take note of the emergency exit locations." — Notice them, remember them.

Of note: Significant, worth mentioning.
"There were no problems of note."

On a [adjective] note: With a particular quality or feeling at a certain point, especially at the beginning or end of something.
"Let's end on a positive note." / "On a more personal note, I'd like to thank my family."

A note of [something]: A detectable trace of a quality or emotion.
"There was a note of desperation in his request."

Compare notes: When two or more people share and discuss their observations, information, or experiences about the same thing.
"After the meeting, we compared notes to see if we had noticed the same things."

Strike a note (or strike the right/wrong note): To create a particular impression or feeling — correctly or incorrectly suited to a situation.
"His apology struck the right note — it felt sincere." / "Her jokes struck a wrong note at the funeral."

Worthy of note: Deserving attention; significant enough to be mentioned.
"One fact worthy of note is that the building was never finished."
How All These Meanings Fit Together

You might wonder: what do music, paper money, short messages, and feelings have to do with each other?

The thread is this: a note is always something brief, distinct, and meaningful that stands out. A musical note is one clear, distinct sound. A written note is a short, focused message. A note of sadness is a distinct quality that you can detect. A person of note is someone who stands out in their field. A banknote is a distinct, recognized unit of value.

Each meaning takes this same core idea — something precise and noticeable — and applies it to a different domain of life.
A Quick Summary of All the Meanings

• A short written message or record (a note on the fridge; taking notes in class)
  • A brief explanatory comment added to a text (footnotes; editor's notes)
  • A formal written communication (a diplomatic note; a promissory note)
  • Paper money (a ten-pound note)
  • A single musical sound of a specific pitch (playing a note on the piano)
  • A quality or tone that you sense in a voice, atmosphere, smell, or flavour (a note of bitterness; on a high note)
  • Importance or distinction (nothing of note; a scientist of note)
11307:
When something is noteworthy, it means it is worth noticing and paying attention to — because it stands out from the ordinary in some meaningful way.

Think of it this way: Out of the hundreds of things that happen around you every day, most are forgettable and routine. But occasionally, something happens that makes you stop and think, "Wait — that's special. That's significant. That deserves attention." That thing is noteworthy.

The word itself is almost self-explanatory once you break it down: note (to notice or pay attention to) + worthy (deserving of). So literally, it means deserving to be noticed.

Something is noteworthy when it rises above the average or the expected. It doesn't have to be shocking or extraordinary — it just has to be meaningfully better, more impressive, more interesting, or more significant than what is normal or typical.

It can be used to describe:

  • A person's achievement — A student who scores full marks in a famously difficult exam has a noteworthy result.
  • An event — A small town suddenly producing three world-class athletes in one year is a noteworthy event.
  • A quality or feature — A phone with a battery that lasts a full week has a noteworthy battery life.
  • Progress or change — A country that reduced its crime rate by 40% in two years has made noteworthy progress.
  • A fact or detail — In a discussion about history, a surprising connection between two events might be called a noteworthy detail.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

"Noteworthy" carries a positive or neutral-but-important tone. When someone calls something noteworthy, they are saying it genuinely deserves your attention — not out of gossip or sensationalism, but because it holds real significance or merit.

It is a calm, respectful, and slightly formal word. You would hear it more in writing, news, academic discussions, professional reviews, or speeches than in casual everyday conversation. If a friend texts you about a movie, they'd probably say "it was really good" — but a film critic writing a review might call the director's technique noteworthy.

"Noteworthy" sits at a moderate-to-high level on the scale of praise or significance. It is stronger than words like fine, decent, or interesting, but it is not as extreme as extraordinary, groundbreaking, or historic.

Here's a rough sense of the scale:

  • Ordinary → fine / decent
  • Above average → good / commendable
  • Clearly stands out → noteworthy ✓
  • Exceptional → remarkable / outstanding
  • Once-in-a-generation → extraordinary / historic

So when you call something noteworthy, you are making a meaningful claim — you're saying it genuinely stands out — but you're not necessarily saying it changed the world.

These examples will show you how the word feels in real use:

  • "The young chef's ability to combine unexpected flavours was particularly noteworthy."
  • "The report highlighted several noteworthy trends in global temperatures."
  • "His calm and composed performance under pressure was noteworthy, especially given his age."
  • "Among all the paintings in the gallery, one stood out as truly noteworthy — its detail was unlike anything else on display."
  • "The company made a noteworthy improvement in customer satisfaction this year."

Notice how in every case, the word signals: pay attention here — this is above average and deserves recognition.

Understanding the edges of a word helps you use it correctly.

  • It is not the same as "famous." A person can be famous for being a celebrity without having done anything noteworthy. And someone can do something deeply noteworthy without being famous at all.
  • It is not the same as "shocking" or "controversial." A scandal might be shocking, but "noteworthy" implies genuine merit or significance, not just surprise or drama.
  • It is not the same as "perfect." Something can be flawed overall but still have a noteworthy quality or aspect.
  • It is not about personal opinion alone. When you say something is noteworthy, you are implying that most reasonable people paying attention would agree it stands out — it's not just your personal taste.

• Remarkable — Very similar to noteworthy, but slightly stronger and often more personal in tone. Something remarkable tends to genuinely surprise or impress you.
  • Significant — Focuses more on importance or impact rather than being impressive. A significant event matters; a noteworthy event both matters and stands out.
  • Notable — Almost identical in meaning to noteworthy. If there's any difference, "notable" tends to be used for things or people that are well-known or recognized, while "noteworthy" focuses slightly more on the quality of deserving attention.
  • Outstanding — Stronger than noteworthy. Something outstanding is exceptionally good, often the best among a group.
  • Commendable — Means deserving praise, but implies a lower bar than noteworthy. You might commend someone for trying hard even if results were average.

Noteworthy describes something that is genuinely above the ordinary — significant, impressive, or interesting enough that it deserves to be noticed, mentioned, and remembered. It is a calm but meaningful word of recognition, used when something rises clearly above the average without necessarily being the most extreme or dramatic thing in the world.

If you ever wonder whether to use it, ask yourself: "Would a thoughtful, reasonable person — not just me — look at this and say, 'That's worth paying attention to'?" If yes, noteworthy is the right word.
11308:
A notion is a vague, general idea or belief that exists in someone's mind — one that is often loosely held, not fully worked out, and not necessarily proven to be true.

The single most important thing to understand about this word is the quality of vagueness it carries. A notion is not a deep, carefully reasoned conclusion. It is more like a rough mental impression — something you think or believe, but haven't fully examined or confirmed.

Sense 1 — A vague idea or belief (the most common meaning)

This is the everyday use of the word. When someone has a notion about something, they have a general feeling or loose understanding of it — not a firm, certain knowledge.

Examples:

  • "She had a notion that something was wrong, but she couldn't explain why."
  • "He had no notion of how serious the situation was."
  • "I have some notion of what the job involves, but I'm not entirely sure."

Notice how in each of these, the person knows something, but it is hazy, incomplete, or unconfirmed. That fuzziness is at the heart of "notion."

Sense 2 — A sudden desire, impulse, or whim

Sometimes "notion" refers to a sudden, spontaneous urge to do something — an impulse that comes without much planning or reasoning behind it.

Examples:

  • "I had a notion to just pack my bags and travel."
  • "She took a notion to rearrange all the furniture."
  • "He woke up one morning with the notion to learn guitar."

In this sense, the notion is an unplanned, spur-of-the-moment feeling — not a well-thought-out decision.

Sense 3 — Notions (plural): small everyday items

In this specific, more narrow use — mainly in American English — notions refers to small useful items sold in a shop, typically related to sewing and clothing repair: things like buttons, needles, thread, pins, ribbons, and zippers. You might see a section in a fabric store labeled "Notions." This is a very specialized use and you will mostly encounter it in retail or sewing contexts.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

Understanding how a word feels in a sentence is just as important as knowing its definition. Here is what you need to know about "notion":

It signals uncertainty or incompleteness. When you use "notion," you are indirectly telling your listener that the idea is not airtight. Saying "I have a notion that..." is softer and more humble than saying "I believe that..." or "I know that..."

It can carry a slightly old-fashioned or literary tone. You will often find "notion" in books, formal writing, and speeches. In casual everyday speech, people might instead say "idea," "feeling," or "thought." However, "notion" is absolutely used in modern everyday English — it simply has a slightly more elevated or thoughtful sound to it.

It is neutral in itself, but the surrounding words shape whether it sounds positive or negative.

  • "a beautiful notion" — sounds positive, almost poetic
  • "a dangerous notion" — sounds negative
  • "a ridiculous notion" — sounds dismissive

These words are close in meaning to "notion," but each one has a slightly different weight.

Notion vs. Idea
An idea is broader and more neutral. It can be specific, detailed, and well-formed. A notion, on the other hand, leans toward the vague and incomplete. Every notion is an idea, but not every idea is a notion.

Notion vs. Concept
A concept is a more formal, well-defined mental category — often used in academic, scientific, or professional language. A notion is looser and more personal. You might study the concept of gravity in a physics class, but you might have a notion that the weather seems to be changing.

Notion vs. Opinion
An opinion is a view or judgment you openly hold and are willing to stand behind. A notion is less committed — you might not even be ready to defend it, because it is still vague in your own mind.

Notion vs. Belief
A belief is something you hold with confidence and conviction. A notion is weaker — you suspect something or have a rough sense of it, but you are not fully certain.
Common Phrases and Patterns You Will Encounter

These are the natural combinations in which you will often see "notion" used:

  • "have a notion" — "I have a notion that things will work out."
  • "no notion of" — "She had no notion of the trouble ahead." (means she was completely unaware)
  • "some notion of" — "Do you have some notion of what you want to do?" (means a rough idea)
  • "the notion that..." — "The notion that hard work always pays off is widely believed." (introduces an idea that is then discussed or challenged)
  • "preconceived notion" — A belief you already held before encountering new information, often one that turns out to be wrong or oversimplified. "Try to let go of your preconceived notions and look at the facts."
  • "romantic notion" — An idealized, dreamy, or unrealistic idea about something. "He had romantic notions about life in the countryside."
  • "challenge/dismiss/reject the notion" — "Scientists dismissed the notion that the drug was safe."
  • "entertain a notion" — To consider or think about an idea, even if you haven't accepted it yet. "She began to entertain the notion of starting her own business."
A Summary to Lock It In

Think of a notion as an idea that lives in the early, misty stage of thought — not yet sharp, not yet proven, not yet fully formed. It's the mental sketch before the detailed painting. It can be a hazy belief you carry about the world, a sudden impulse to do something, or (in a very specific context) a small household item in a fabric store.

When you see or hear "notion," ask yourself: "Is someone expressing a loose, unconfirmed idea here?" — and the answer will almost always be yes.
11309:
Start here, because everything else builds on this.

A notion is a thought, idea, or concept — something that lives in the mind. So, something notional belongs to the world of ideas and concepts rather than to concrete, practical reality. It exists "in theory" or "on paper," but the real world may tell a different story.

The key tension the word carries is this: there is often a gap between the notional version of something and the actual version. The notional version is tidy and theoretical; the real version may be messier, different in practice, or may not fully exist at all.
Meaning 1: Existing Only in Theory, Not in Reality

This is the most common use. Something notional has been designated, assigned, or agreed upon as a concept — but it doesn't fully hold up in the real world.

Examples:

  • "The treaty gave the rebel group notional control over the northern province." — On paper, they had control. In practice, the region was contested and ungoverned.
  • "He had a notional budget of $5,000 for the project, though everyone knew the actual costs would be far higher." — The figure existed as a planning number, not as a reflection of reality.
  • "The country achieved notional independence in 1960, but foreign powers still directed its economy." — Independence existed as a concept and a label; real self-governance did not.

You will very often see "notional" paired with words like value, control, authority, independence, figure, price — all things that can exist as official designations while the reality is quite different.
Meaning 2: Vague, Speculative, or at the Idea Stage

Notional can describe plans, timelines, or proposals that are approximate, unconfirmed, or still just floating ideas — not yet grounded in firm decisions or facts.

Examples:

  • "We have a notional plan for the event, but nothing has been confirmed yet."
  • "The architect sketched a notional layout for the new building — just to give the client a rough sense of the space."
  • "Her retirement date was notional; she hadn't actually decided."

Here, "notional" signals: don't take this as fixed or final. It's a placeholder, a starting point, a rough shape of an idea.
Meaning 3: In Finance — Notional Value or Notional Amount

This is a very precise, technical use you'll encounter frequently in finance, economics, and business writing.

In financial contracts — especially instruments like derivatives, swaps, and options — the notional value (also called the notional amount or notional principal) is the theoretical face value used to calculate payments. Crucially, this is not the actual amount of money that changes hands.

Here's a simple example: Suppose two banks enter into an interest rate swap with a notional principal of $10 million. Neither bank actually pays the other $10 million. Instead, they exchange interest payments calculated based on that $10 million. The $10 million is a reference number — it exists only as the agreed-upon base for the math, not as real cash being transferred.

This is why the word "notional" fits perfectly: the value is real as a concept and as a calculating tool, but it is not real as money that moves.

  • "The total notional value of the derivatives market runs into the hundreds of trillions of dollars — far exceeding the actual GDP of the world."

When you read about financial markets and see astronomically large figures, they are almost always notional values, not actual money in circulation.

In language study, "notional" refers to meaning or concept, as opposed to grammatical structure or function.

A notional definition defines something by what it means. The classic example is the definition of a noun many of us learned in school: "A noun is a person, place, or thing." That is a notional definition — it tells you what nouns refer to conceptually. A formal definition, by contrast, describes how a noun behaves in a sentence (it can be a subject or object, it takes plural endings, etc.).

Notional grammar is an approach to describing language that organizes words and categories around their meanings — what they express conceptually — rather than around their structural roles. It's the older, more intuitive approach to grammar, and it's been debated by linguists who prefer more rigorous structural analysis.
Meaning 5: Fanciful or Whimsical (Older / Literary Use)

In older English texts and literature, calling someone's ideas — or the person themselves — "notional" carried the flavour of overly imaginative, full of whims, or impractically theoretical. It suggested someone who lived too much in the world of notions and not enough in the world of facts and practical realities.

This meaning is rarely used in modern writing, but you may come across it in 18th- or 19th-century literature. If you do, think of it as: "fanciful, airy, not grounded in reality."

Every use of "notional" shares the same thread: it points away from the concrete and actual, toward the conceptual and theoretical. Whether it's a notional figure in a budget (theoretical), a notional plan (vague and unconfirmed), a notional financial value (a reference number, not real cash), a notional grammar definition (based on concept, not structure), or a notional idea in old literature (fanciful and impractical) — the word consistently marks something as belonging to the world of ideas, not the world of things.

Whenever you encounter "notional," ask yourself: "What would the real or actual version of this look like?" That question will almost always reveal the gap the word is pointing to — the gap between the concept and the reality. The notional version is the conceptual, theoretical, on-paper one; the actual version is what truly exists or happens.

The most natural antonyms of notional are actual, real, concrete, and tangible. Its closest synonyms, depending on context, include theoretical, hypothetical, conceptual, abstract, putative, and nominal (though each of these has its own distinct shade of meaning).
